artist: Guy Blackman & Ben O’Connor / Chapter Music
title: Breaking And Entering: Guy Blackman and Ben O’Connor On Chapter Music’s Iconic Catalog and Their Final Releases
summary: After 30 years and over 200 releases, beloved independent label Chapter Music are releasing their final new records. Founder, Guy Blackman and co-founder, Ben O’Connor, take a look back on the label’s evolution from their DIY beginnings at RTRFM in Perth to their latest release with Teether & Kuya Neil. Listen in to hear Guy and Ben open up about the different scenes the label’s adapted to and the legacy that Chapter Music will leave.
transcript:
Guy Blackman and Ben O’Connor discuss Chapter Music’s catalogue and final new releases on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 22 May 2025.

Thank you for having us.

Hello.

Well, it's a bittersweet moment for us as we, of course, celebrate the legacy of the incredible Chapter Music. And before we get into some questions, I guess we really do have to gush because this is an emotional moment for us. For those, I suppose, coming to Chapter Music more recently, you have both spent 33 years essentially shaping the sounds of this country's independent music scene. What began, Guy, as a personal project to document your immediate community evolved into a powerhouse label that's been responsible for launching countless careers. We heard Laura Jean in there. Of course, there's Twerps, Goon Sax, Teether and Kuya Neil. Too many more. We worked out that there's pretty much a Chapter Music band for every letter of the alphabet, which is very appropriate given the literary ties of the label name. Your unique approach has led you to consciously champion a really diverse range of artists and you've built the world that you want to see, which is inclusive, artist-driven and community-focused. It's such a thrill to have you with us.

I guess we also wanted to ask, how are you feeling on the eve of this farewell show and the beginning of a new chapter?

Yeah, it's strange, obviously. We're going through lots of mixed emotions, the happy and the sad. It's very bittersweet. But we're feeling very zen, I think, overall.

I'm just feeling a little bit kind of touched by, you know, kind of grateful or whatever, you know, feeling very spiritual about just how much amazing music we've gotten to be involved in over the years and how lucky we are to have worked with so many incredible artists.

That's beautiful. And so, yeah, you mentioned some messages, people have been reaching out, artists and fans. Are you comfortable sort of sharing maybe some of the things you're hearing from people?

I don't know, like...

No, sorry, it's probably a bit difficult.

It has been really lovely having both, like, kind of people we don't know message us but also, I guess, yeah, it's really meaningful having, like, a bunch of bands and artists that we've worked with kind of getting in touch and saying nice things.

That's lovely.

Yeah, we sent out a big email, like, you know, at the start of the year or some stage, you know, warning people, you know, making a kind of an official announcement to the artists that this was happening. And, yeah, like, you know, did get so many, you know, nice replies. You know, like there's artists that we haven't, you know, put a record out, you know, for like decades, you know, artists we worked with in the 90s or the 2000s, you know, that we still really love and, you know, whose music is still kind of, you know, on the, you know, the Chapter catalogue. And, yeah, so it's just a lot of people across a long time and, yeah, it was quite kind of, you know, overwhelming getting a bit of an influx all at once, once we sent that message, you know, from everyone being like, oh, you know, sorry to hear this and thanks, you know, and loved working with you, et cetera, et cetera.

I'm not much of a nostalgic person generally, but it has been pretty kind of like overwhelming over the last like month or so.

Absolutely. Well, the influence and, yeah, legacy is enormous and really reaches into every corner of the music, yeah, community here, which is so special.

Yeah.

And I guess for regular RRR listeners, the story of Chapter Music would be a familiar one, but maybe for those who've discovered your releases more recently, maybe we'd like to go back to, you know, the early days and where it all started. You said previously that running a label is about creating the world that you want to see, a world where art and individual expression are paramount and where community is incredibly important. I think that might have been you that said that, Ben. Could you maybe expand on how this personal philosophy shaped Chapter Music's roster and its overall identity over the decades?

Well, I guess the, I think initially it maybe wasn't as kind of intentional or conscious. And like, I think it was definitely kind of like, you know, when Guy started the label, it was very much about documenting his immediate community.

And I think that there are, I don't know, it's difficult to kind of sum up the philosophy of it or how these things have come about. Like things like, I guess for, we've released very few acts that are like all straight white men kind of thing. And that was never really an intentional thing originally. It was always just the kind of stuff that we were drawn to before we kind of started realising, oh, this is kind of what we do. And it's obviously not a hard and fast rule. Like we have put out bands of all straight white men because the music they've made is amazing, but it hasn't necessarily always been something that we're drawn to.

But I think just as people, like community has always been important to us. And I think that we're both also people who are really attracted to kind of like very personal expressions that people make. We're really attracted to like art that could only have been made by that particular person.

Yeah.

Anything you want to add, Guy?

I think you said, you know, everything that I was thinking.

I mean, I guess, you know, we were a couple, you know, we've been a couple since, you know, 1995 and, you know, at that time, I guess, you know, there was less visibility for queer artists than there is now. I mean, in some ways it goes up and down. I mean, the 90s were a pretty queer decade too, but, you know, we felt like, you know, we were trying to foreground some voices that weren't as often heard at the time or over the years, you know, like female artists, queer artists, you know, there's always more work to be done, you know, people of colour, you know, trying not to, yeah, just not to kind of contribute to the monolith of kind of, you know, of the kind of standard, you know, Australian kind of rock music or whatever.

Absolutely. I suppose you just talked about, you know, the 90s. And when we look at Chapter Music, obviously it is an institution that spans 33 years and it's an unfolding story because of course it will continue in new forms. But throughout that time, you really have pushed and provided a platform for artists across the spectrum and you've seen a lot of changes in the music industry as well. I guess what the 90s looked like compared to now is profoundly different. Do you sort of identify chapters within the Chapter Music history in certain eras that you can identify clearly? What are some of the chapters?

There's probably, you know, micro chapters.

There's a hundred of them.

Yeah.

I mean, the first few years were the cassette years in Perth when I was a teenager, basically putting out cassette compilations of Perth bands and, and, you know, then I moved to Melbourne in 1995, you know, I'd met Ben like, you know, 1994, very end of 94 or the very start of 95 on a visit over from Perth.

Beautifully documented in Adult Baby as well. Your debut album.

So, yeah, then I guess that mid 90s era, I got a job at the vinyl record pressing factory too. So that was the seven inch vinyl kind of era of the label. And then that kind of lasted, you know, CDs started coming in kind of grudgingly. We were, you know, we were late adopters to CDs because, you know, I was just a big vinyl fanatic and both of us, you know, had a preference.

And then we moved to Japan in the early 2000s. So that was kind of like the first... At that point we were like, the label's finishing, like it had been 10 years and, and, you know, we weren't sure that we were going to keep the label going once we got back. But we, we spent a year and a half in Japan kind of seeing all this amazing Japanese music and that just inspired us as soon as we got back to Australia in 2004 to start putting out some of that Japanese music and documenting that. And then, you know, you know, I've just kind of snowballed again from there.

Absolutely. Since then, I guess, are there other eras?

I guess we were talking a bit about how kind of like right after that, like kind of the late 2000s into the early 2010s was like the blog era. Suddenly all our bands were getting written about by these kind of up and coming music websites from around the world. You know, we weren't really too, you know, aware of the significance of them at first, but like when Pitchfork and The Fader and Stereogum and, you know, all these kind of places started discovering our releases, you know, that kind of...

I think we made a conscious decision to really kind of, like when that started happening, to really kind of chase it.

Yeah, we did start. I mean, I guess, yeah.

At that time, I knew it was hard to get attention for the kind of Australian music that we were interested in, like, in Australia.

Apart from community radio.

Yeah, apart from RRR and other community stations.

So, yeah, we were, you know, kind of trying to sidestep the accepted avenues by like going overseas and getting, you know, getting, you know, these tastemakers to get excited about Chapter and then that would in turn, you know, get other people back here excited about us.

Often the way it works with, like, the wider Australian music industry, obviously there's that kind of, like, there's the underground and then there's the kind of, like, community radio, which has always supported, like, interesting shit, interesting stuff that is going on here. Pardon my French.

No.

But I think there's always...

You're allowed to say the word. I've said much worse on this radio station before.

I, yeah, like, I think that there's always been a thing that the wider Australian music industry doesn't start paying attention to interesting Australian music until it starts getting attention overseas.

Yeah.

So, we were like, let's just go straight overseas.

Yeah.

Planting those seeds.

So, yeah, bands like Crayon Fields and Fabulous Diamonds and then Twerps and Dick Diver all kind of started to benefit from that and, you know, that, I guess that was an era. I'm not sure when that came to an end, sometime in the mid-2010s or something.

Yeah. And since then, what's the last 10 years been?

I don't know.

Just Chapter's adult era.

I'm a little aged.

Just triumph after triumph, basically.

If you've just joined us, we've got Guy Blackman and Ben O'Connor from Chapter Music with us in the studio ahead of the End of an Era party, which is happening as part of RISING at Max Watt’s on Friday, June 7.

[Unclear audio at 00:11:27–00:16:26]

I think maybe we had a little bit of, you know, some kind of idea of creating some kind of, you know, some vibe. I don't know.

It [Unclear audio at 00:16:35–00:16:38] captured your time and place in Melbourne. That's for sure.

Absolutely.

And of course, yeah, there have been so many incredible Chapter releases and a real sort of victory lap of, um, final new releases as well with Teether and Kuya Neil's new album and a great new EP from Npcede as well, and of course, Guy, your own, uh, second album which is very exciting. Can you maybe tell us a bit more about these and what they say about the, um, depth and breadth of the label?

Um, I guess, yeah, the Teether and Kuya Neil record is a really kind of, you know, it's a really satisfying kind of culmination of the relationship we've had with them for the last four years or so, you know, we were really kind of... You know, Ben was like... I think Ben heard them on Triple R.

I did. I heard them on Good Static for the first time, a song from their first EP. And from the very first time I heard it, I was just like, we have to work with these.

And I was like, they're not going to want to work with us. Well, you know, we're like, you know, we're old and, you know, old white dags, you know, put out lots of, lots of, you know, non-hip-hop music. And then, but then we set up a meeting with them, and yeah, immediately we just found, like, you know, we had so much in common that we didn't realise we were going to, and, you know, so much... Such a similar approach to the way we do things that it just kind of seemed to gel and became this really beautiful relationship.

So yeah, like, working towards their debut album after, like, the two mixtapes we've done, you know, it's been a real, real kind of big, long, complicated and rewarding process.

They've been thrilled with the relationship as well, of course. We were very fortunate to speak with Kuya Neil a couple of weeks ago about the brilliant new album.

Yeah, it's like the best hip-hop record ever made in this country, I reckon.

It is, like, it's... I feel like that maybe we're not, you know... Are we the most qualified people to make that statement? I don't know.

I feel like that's a... Yeah, that's a pretty definitive statement to make. I think that's really an extraordinary record which really breaks so many boundaries and includes so many different sort of international but very hyper local styles as well.

One thing we love discovering during the interview was about you, Ben, and Kuya Neil was saying how good you are at sequencing records. So when did you know you had the superpower?

I can't remember what the first record we put out that I sequenced was, but I think it was something that I always used to do just when people were sending us, like, if people would kind of send demos or tracks through before they'd completed the record or whatever, I would always make playlists of how I liked listening to them. And quite often bands would be like, we're not exactly sure the sequence we want to go with this record.

I'd be like, [Unclear audio at 00:19:13–00:19:15].

I'm sure.

It's... I don't know. It's like, yeah, I'm not sure, I can't remember. I have no idea what the first record...

You are really good at it though.

[Unclear audio at 00:19:22–00:19:26] Like, I've probably done it for a lot.

That's awesome.

That we have... Like, you know, lots of acts will have, like, this is, this is definitely how we want it, and we know. And I don't ever want to interfere with that if someone has, like, their own vision. But if someone, like, asks for help or is, like, is kind of, you know, prevaricating and not making decisions, then...

Yeah, happy to bring your sort of like impeccable ears to the project and, yeah, make some decisions.

And with Npcede, I guess that was just something we were really, really excited about the idea of kind of going out with a bang and doing something really unexpected as one of our final releases. We were already kind of quite well advanced into the mechanics in our head of kind of how this was going to happen when we saw their very first show, like a year ago, two years ago.

You know, we already knew that this was, you know, on the cards, but we were like, why don't we sign this artist and release their debut record as one of our very final releases, you know. It was just... I think we saw them and were just completely gobsmacked and blown away within like a minute of their set starting, and then progressively as the set went on and we saw, like, just how good and how interesting they were for like a band playing their first ever show. We just, like, we have to, like... We were talking about it while they were playing, kind of thinking, like, we have to talk to [Unclear audio at 00:20:41–00:20:45] and we have to kind of...

It's quite liberating, really, like, let's put out, you know, a record, and then just, you know, they can go off and do whatever they want, you know. We don't have the attachments, you know. They can... We're basically proffering them up on a silver platter to the rest of the music world to be like, look at this incredible band. You should, you know, you should snatch them away from us and sign them and make them mega famous, you know.

Fantastic. I'm sure you may work together in various capacities.

I just think that they're a band that could be enormous like that.

I think they're one of the most exciting bands in the world. They're just phenomenal, and kind of seeing the kind of progression that they've had over the time that we've known them has been astounding.

So there's that trajectory, definitely.

Yeah.

And then I guess my solo album had to come last, really, because I just wouldn't have been able to kind of focus on it, you know, with all the other stuff going on. And, you know, I made a solo album like 15 years ago. You know, I came back from Japan in 2004, like all revved up, like, you know, this is my time to be a solo guy and make my statement as an artist. And it took me like three or four years to put that record out. 

And then after that I was like, oh, that was exhausting and confronting, and, you know, putting yourself out into the world as a songwriter and a performer is scary. 

Especially in the late 2000s as a gay songwriter writing these really kind of personal gay songs. I was like, this is, you know... People aren't responding. People are still uncomfortable. I'm making them uncomfortable and that's making me uncomfortable.

But, you know, a lot's changed since then, and, you know, I kind of... The end of the record label or that, you know, this transition is partly also just to remind myself that I'm, you know, I'm an artist and a musician too. So I wanted the record to have a little bit of space at the end of the label to kind of, you know, have its own moment. 

And it's been... It's a really nice feeling to have a record out again finally. I gave up thinking that it would ever happen for a long time. 

So, you know, it's nice to, you know... I guess when I started, when we started Chapter, you know, like, it was very natural for me to be playing music and putting out other people's music. It was very low, low-stakes cassettes and the occasional seven inch and everyone was just all friends and we were all the kids, you know. But as things went on it just, you know, became more complicated. So yeah. So it's very nice.

I mean, the label is still going to keep going. I'm not sure how much, you know... Like, reissues used to be, you know, maybe 25 percent of what we were doing. So that's probably going to be... You know, we're going to keep going at a quarter of the pace. From now on, you know, we're going to still put out the occasional reissue of old music from the past. But, you know, I think it's just time for us to, you know, have this change.

Yeah, absolutely. And as you say, continuing to platform incredible music to, I suppose, strengthen the connections with the past but also enable us to sort of look ahead through that lens as well. And there was a great article Lauren and I were reading, of course, with Brodie Lancaster in Fairfax Press. Beautiful, recommended reading to anyone who hasn't had a chance to check it out. But I suppose there's one quote from the article, a powerful statement that you made, Ben. What you're trying to do now is show another way of looking at the [Unclear audio at 00:23:57–00:24:02].

I think when I said that, I think we were talking about both the new releases that we're doing. We're talking about Teether and Kuya Neil and Npcede. I think I was also specifically talking about the RISING show that we're doing. Because I guess, like, with the RISING show, we've kind of tried to kind of cover as many bases as possible from what Chapter has been in the past, what it is now, what it could be in the future. 

But also, like, we have a couple of guests who are, like, non-Chapter-related playing the party, like Sidney Phillips, this incredible rapper from Brisbane who I think is moving to Melbourne, if she hasn't already moved, who I am just completely obsessed with. And I think is one of the most exciting things in the country right now.

And we also have, like, a person I think is the best songwriter in the world right now, Ryan Davis from Ryan Davis and the Roadhouse Band.

Excuse me, I'm right here.

One of the top... One of the top three songwriters in the world, alongside Guy Blackman and Lana Del Rey.

I'm happy with that.

And both of those people, I guess, we chose because we love the music that they make, but also, like, Sidney has her own collective stealthyn00b, that's kind of like a bunch of rappers and producers, most of them are from Brisbane, I think. And Ryan has his own label, Sophomore Lounge. And it's kind of... Kind of wanted to kind of connect to other, you know... We might be ending, but there's so many interesting things happening here and around the world if you just look for them a little bit.

Well, the End of an Era show is happening at Max Watt’s on Friday the 7th of June as part of RISING's Day Tripper Festival. A huge lineup. Do you want to talk us through the rest of the lineup?

It's the greatest hits set.

Yeah, I think I'll sneak some copies of the record onto the merch desk for the RISING show a week before, so if you want a special preview copy come to Max Watt’s on the 7th of June between the hours of 12 and 8pm.

It'll be a joyous and emotional occasion.

Absolutely.

Thanks so much, Guy and Ben for joining us.
